rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify poorly resolved pairs while aiming for a short run. The retention pattern will guide window trimming and subsequent slope and temperature adjustments.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded central peaks respond to a shallower slope. The current last-peak time leaves room to improve resolution without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The limiting pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further. Raising the starting organic fraction slightly should offset the longer gradient and keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes while retaining ample separation of the early peaks.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. The slightly shallower gradient should preserve the limiting pair’s resolution, while the early peaks have ample separation margin.

Injection 4 reached the maximum possible CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a 5 °C increase to shorten retention while checking whether temperature preserves or improves the limiting pair’s resolution.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the limiting pair through an elution-order crossover and restores separation while shortening the run. Injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Lengthen the gradient slightly to improve the new limiting pair at 55 °C, which is just below baseline resolution. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves room for this adjustment while targeting full resolution within 10 minutes.
Use a slope between injections 6 and 7 to retain full resolution while shortening the last-peak time. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves selectivity for the limiting middle pair enough to tolerate a steeper, shorter gradient. Injection 8 remains a fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Shorten only the gradient duration to test whether injection 9’s full resolution can be retained with earlier elution. This isolates slope sensitivity at the promising lower starting organic fraction.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test whether the selectivity improvement seen in injection 9 can rescue the limiting pair at a 12-minute gradient. Monitor the other close central pair, whose resolution margin is small.

Test a hotter, steeper gradient for a shorter fully resolved separation, checking whether the temperature shift creates new central co-elutions. Injection 11 remains the shortest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity regime, where central peak reordering may permit full resolution with a shorter gradient. The broad window should retain all compounds, and injection 11 remains the shortest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction at 60 °C separates the central pair on the opposite side of its apparent selectivity crossover. This could yield a faster maximum-score method, but early-peak compression must also be checked.

Lower the starting organic fraction to restore early-pair resolution, and test a steeper gradient to move the central pair farther from its apparent crossover. This explores a faster separation while retaining injection 11 as the shortest proven maximum-score method.

Target a slope between injections 9 and 10 to balance the two limiting central pairs with a shorter programmed gradient. This aims to retain the maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 11.

Test the unexplored 50 °C selectivity regime with a short gradient, looking for a balance between the central-pair crossovers observed at higher temperatures. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention, while previously demonstrated maximum-score methods remain available.

Preserve injection 11’s successful gradient slope while trimming the final organic fraction above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction of 0.57. This should retain maximum CRF with an 8-minute programmed gradient.

Shift injection 4’s gradient window upward while preserving its slope to test whether full resolution survives with earlier elution. Check both early-peak compression and the limiting central pair; the maximum-score methods already demonstrated remain available.

Test the unexplored 35 °C selectivity regime with a moderate gradient to see whether it separates the central cluster faster than the proven 40 °C method. Maximum CRF is already secured, so this run explores an alternative rather than replacing the established methods.

Increase the slope modestly from the shortest proven fully resolved method to test its speed limit. This should shorten retention, with the central pair previously at R = 1.59 most likely to become limiting.

Test whether further steepening at 60 °C improves the central crossover pair enough to achieve a substantially faster fully resolved separation. Monitor the neighboring pair, which had only a small resolution margin in injection 15; the established maximum-score methods remain the fallback.
